landmark-001.summary: An iron lattice structure built in Paris for the 1889 World's Fair.
facts: It was originally meant to be a temporary structure standing for only 20 years.
After dark, 20,000 lights sparkle for five minutes at the top of every hour.

landmark-002.summary: A monumental arch that Napoleon commissioned at the end of the Champs-Élysées in Paris to celebrate his victory at Austerlitz.
facts: Construction began in 1806 and finished in 1836, so Napoleon never saw it completed.
Climb its 284 steps and you'll see twelve grand avenues radiating out like a star.

landmark-003.summary: An art museum opened in 1793 by the revolutionary government in a converted former royal palace in Paris.
facts: It is home to the “Mona Lisa” and the Venus de Milo.
Its glass pyramid entrance, opened in 1989, was designed by architect I. M. Pei.

landmark-004.summary: An abbey founded in 708 by Bishop Aubert on a rocky tidal island off the coast of Normandy.
facts: During the Hundred Years' War, it held out against an English siege to the very end.
The old causeway was removed and replaced with a bridge, so it becomes an island again at high spring tides.

landmark-005.summary: The great bell that has rung out the hours from the clock tower of London's Houses of Parliament since 1859.
facts: It weighs 13.7 tons and fell almost silent during a five-year restoration that began in 2017.
The tower's official name, Elizabeth Tower, was given in 2012 to mark the Queen's Diamond Jubilee.

landmark-006.summary: A bridge across the Thames in London, completed in 1894, whose center opens to let ships pass.
facts: It takes its name from the Tower of London, which stands right beside it.
Glass floors added to the upper walkways in 2014 let you look down at the river 42 meters below.

landmark-007.summary: A prehistoric ring of huge standing stones raised on Salisbury Plain c. 2500 BC.
facts: Visitors normally view it from behind a fence, but at dawn on the summer solstice they can walk among the stones to greet the sunrise.
Many of the smaller bluestones were hauled from Wales, more than 200 kilometers away.

landmark-008.summary: An aristocrat's mansion in London, enlarged into a palace that has been the British monarch's residence since 1837.
facts: The Changing of the Guard takes place in front of the main gates at 11 a.m., almost daily in summer.
When the monarch is in residence, the Royal Standard flies overhead.

landmark-009.summary: An arena built in Rome around AD 80, where more than 50,000 spectators watched gladiator fights.
facts: It appears on Italy's 5-cent euro coin.
Emperor Titus opened it with 100 days of games.

landmark-010.summary: A cathedral campanile, begun in 1173, that tilts to one side because of the soft ground beneath it.
facts: Today you can climb 296 slanting steps up to the belfry at the top.
It closed in 1990 for 11 years of stabilization work that reduced its tilt from 5.5 to 4 degrees.

landmark-011.summary: A Baroque fountain in Rome designed by Nicola Salvi, begun in 1732 and completed in 1762.
facts: Legend says tossing a coin over your shoulder ensures you'll return to Rome; the money collected goes to the charity Caritas.
It is still fed by the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built in 19 BC.

landmark-012.summary: The main square of Venice, framed by a basilica glittering with gold mosaics and a tall bell tower.
facts: Napoleon is said to have called it “the most beautiful drawing room in Europe.”
Between fall and spring, high tides known as acqua alta flood the square.

landmark-013.summary: A Gothic cathedral in northern Italy with 135 spires rising like a forest.
facts: Construction began in 1386, and it was not officially completed until 1965.
With a ticket, you can go up to the rooftop terraces and stroll among the spires.

landmark-014.summary: A Roman city near Naples buried whole under ash from Mount Vesuvius in AD 79.
facts: Stone shop counters with built-in food jars still line its streets.
Systematic excavation began in 1748.

landmark-015.summary: A Barcelona basilica designed by Antoni Gaudí, begun in 1882 and still under construction today.
facts: Antoni Gaudí was struck by a tram and killed in 1926, never seeing it finished.
In February 2026, its central Tower of Jesus reached 172.5 meters, making it the tallest church in the world.

landmark-016.summary: A red fortress that the Nasrid dynasty began building on a hill in Granada in 1238.
facts: After visiting, Francisco Tárrega composed the guitar piece “Recuerdos de la Alhambra.”
Its surrender by the last Muslim dynasty in 1492 marked the end of the Reconquista.

landmark-017.summary: A park covered in colorful tiles, laid out by Antoni Gaudí on a Barcelona hillside between 1900 and 1914.
facts: It was originally planned as an upscale housing estate before becoming a park.
The tiled lizard on the entrance stairway, El Drac, is always crowded with people taking photos.

landmark-018.summary: An art museum opened in Madrid in 1819 to house the Spanish royal collection.
facts: Its walls hold Diego Velázquez's “Las Meninas” and Goya's “The Third of May 1808.”
During the last two hours before closing, the permanent collection is free to visit.

landmark-019.summary: A fortress built around 1519 by Manuel I at the mouth of the Tagus River in Lisbon.
facts: Ships setting out on the sea route to India sailed right past it.
In 1983, it became a World Heritage Site together with the Jerónimos Monastery.

landmark-020.summary: A city gate erected in Berlin in 1791 by the Prussian king, modeled on the monumental gateway of a temple in Athens.
facts: It appears on Germany's 10-, 20- and 50-cent euro coins.
In December 1989, the gate, long blocked by the Berlin Wall, reopened after 28 years.

landmark-021.summary: A castle that Ludwig II began building in 1869 on a rocky Alpine hill near Füssen.
facts: It was still unfinished when the king died in 1886, and it opened to visitors just seven weeks later.
It is often cited as the model for the Disney castle.

landmark-022.summary: A Gothic cathedral, begun in 1248 and finished 632 years later, that was once the tallest building in the world.
facts: It took 14 bomb hits during World War II and still did not collapse.
With no elevator, visitors climb 533 steps to the south tower's viewing platform, about 100 meters up.

landmark-023.summary: The Baroque summer palace of the Habsburgs on the outskirts of Vienna.
facts: It has 1,441 rooms, and its grounds hold the world's oldest zoo, opened in 1752.
In 1762, a six-year-old Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart performed for the empress in its Hall of Mirrors.

landmark-024.summary: A castle begun around 880 on a hill above the Vltava River that grew into one of the largest in the world.
facts: Every day at noon, a grand Changing of the Guard takes place in the first courtyard by the main gate.
Once the seat of the kings of Bohemia, it now houses the office of the Czech president.

landmark-025.summary: A stone bridge over the Vltava, begun in 1357 and lined with thirty statues of saints.
facts: Legend says touching the relief of St. John of Nepomuk on the bridge will make your wish come true.
Until 1841, it was the only bridge across the Vltava in Prague.

landmark-026.summary: A temple to Athena that the people of Athens began building on the Acropolis in 447 BC.
facts: About half of its sculptures were removed in the early 19th century by the British diplomat Lord Elgin and are now in the British Museum.
Its columns bulge slightly in the middle so that they appear perfectly straight.

landmark-027.summary: A volcanic island in the Aegean Sea, its clifftops lined with white walls and blue domes.
facts: Around 1600 BC, a massive eruption collapsed the center of the island, leaving it crescent-shaped.
Every evening, crowds gather on the cliffs of Oia to watch the sunset.

landmark-028.summary: A cathedral built in 1561 on Red Square in Moscow by Ivan IV to commemorate the conquest of Kazan.
facts: Legend says the architect was blinded so he could never build anything like it again, but there is no evidence for this.
Its vivid colors are the result of repeated repainting from the 1680s to 1848.

landmark-029.summary: An art museum in Saint Petersburg whose galleries fill the tsars' former Winter Palace.
facts: It began in 1764 with 225 paintings purchased by Catherine II.
Dozens of cats, first brought in to catch mice, still live in its basements.

landmark-030.summary: A domed building in Istanbul built in 537 by Emperor Justinian and now used as a mosque.
facts: It became a mosque in 1453 and a museum in 1935, then was converted back into a mosque in 2020.
Since January 2024, foreign tourists pay a 25-euro admission fee.

landmark-031.summary: A high plateau dotted with mushroom-shaped rock formations and cave dwellings.
facts: People carved underground cities out of rock formed from hardened volcanic ash.
Every morning at dawn, dozens of hot-air balloons rise into the sky together.

landmark-032.summary: A 4,478-meter pyramid-shaped peak with four knife-edged faces on the border of Switzerland and Italy.
facts: Until 2023, it was pictured on the packaging of Toblerone chocolate.
Edward Whymper's party of seven made the first ascent in 1865, but four of them died on the way down.

landmark-033.summary: A snowy Alpine peak where a cogwheel railway tunnels through the mountain up to a high saddle.
facts: Opened in 1912, the station on the saddle sits at 3,454 meters, the highest railway station in Europe.
The Aletsch Glacier, the longest in the Alps, stretches out beside it.

landmark-034.summary: The heart of the Catholic Church, consecrated in Vatican City in 1626 after 120 years of construction.
facts: Michelangelo designed its dome, and Bernini designed the oval square in front of it.
At Easter and Christmas, the pope blesses the crowds in the square from the central balcony.

landmark-035.summary: A chapel inside the Vatican's Apostolic Palace, built in 1481 by Pope Sixtus IV.
facts: Starting in 1508, Michelangelo spent four years painting its ceiling frescoes of the Creation.
During a conclave, white smoke rising from its chimney means a new pope has been elected.

landmark-036.summary: A bronze figure placed on a rock by the Copenhagen waterfront in 1913 to honor a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.
facts: Carl Jacobsen, son of the founder of Carlsberg, commissioned it after falling in love with a ballet based on the story.
Standing just 1.25 meters tall, it surprises many first-time visitors with its small size.

landmark-037.summary: A deep, narrow fjord where the Seven Sisters waterfall tumbles down the cliffs.
facts: On the opposite cliff stands the Suitor waterfall, facing the Sisters.
It was designated a World Natural Heritage Site in 2005.

landmark-038.summary: A milky open-air geothermal spa on a volcanic island, filled with water from a geothermal power plant.
facts: Since 2023, repeated eruptions from nearby volcanoes have forced it to close several times.
Its water looks blue because of the silica it contains.

landmark-039.summary: Fortifications encircling an old Adriatic port city, built between the 13th and 17th centuries.
facts: You can walk a full loop along the top of the roughly 1,940-meter circuit.
It served as a filming location for King's Landing, the capital in the TV series “Game of Thrones.”

landmark-040.summary: A memorial preserving the concentration camp that Nazi Germany set up in southern Poland in 1940.
facts: At least 1.1 million people lost their lives here.
It was liberated by Soviet troops on January 27, 1945, a date now marked as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

landmark-041.summary: A long line of fortifications built along mountain ridges to keep out nomadic peoples from the north.
facts: Successive dynasties added to it, and most of what stands today dates from the Ming dynasty.
The Ming-era sections are usually said to run from Shanhai Pass in the east to Jiayu Pass in the west.

landmark-042.summary: The imperial palace completed in the heart of Beijing in 1420 by the Ming dynasty's Yongle Emperor.
facts: The Palace Museum was established here in 1925, so anyone with a ticket can walk through the palace.
Some 980 buildings survive; the claim that it has 9,999 rooms is an exaggeration.

landmark-043.summary: A host of clay soldiers and horses that Qin Shi Huang had buried beside his tomb near Xi'an.
facts: It was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well.
Every soldier has a different face.

landmark-044.summary: A palace built in tiers on the Red Hill in Lhasa by the Fifth Dalai Lama in 1645.
facts: It stands at an altitude of about 3,700 meters.
It served as the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas until the 1959 exile.

landmark-045.summary: A white marble mausoleum in Agra built by a Mughal emperor in memory of his late wife.
facts: Shah Jahan began it in 1632 and, with some 20,000 artisans, completed it in 1653.
It is closed to tourists on Fridays.

landmark-046.summary: A temple near Siem Reap dedicated to Vishnu by Suryavarman II in the 12th century.
facts: It was built as a Hindu temple and later became a Buddhist one.
It appears on the flag of Cambodia.

landmark-047.summary: The world's largest Buddhist temple, built in central Java by the Sailendra dynasty around the 9th century.
facts: Long forgotten, it was brought to the world's attention in 1814 by the British governor Raffles after he heard reports of it.
Up to 1,200 visitors a day may climb to the top, accompanied by a guide and wearing bamboo sandals.

landmark-048.summary: A pair of 452-meter twin skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1998 and linked by a skybridge.
facts: They were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Their floor plan is based on an eight-pointed Islamic star, and visitors can go up to the skybridge on the 41st floor.

landmark-049.summary: A resort opened on the Singapore waterfront in 2010, with three hotel towers topped by a ship-shaped garden.
facts: Its rooftop pool is about 190 meters above the ground and open only to hotel guests.
Every night, a light-and-water show called Spectra is staged on the bay in front.

landmark-050.summary: A temple built within Bangkok's Grand Palace by Rama I in the late 18th century to enshrine the Emerald Buddha.
facts: Despite its name, the Buddha is carved not from emerald but from green jade or jasper.
Three times a year, at each change of season, the king changes the statue's robes.

landmark-051.summary: A bay where nearly 2,000 limestone islands and rock pillars rise from the sea.
facts: Its name means “where the dragon descended.”
It became a World Natural Heritage Site in 1994.

landmark-052.summary: Japan's highest volcano, rising in a gently sloping cone.
facts: It stands 3,776 meters tall and was named a World Heritage Site in 2013 as a source of faith and artistic inspiration.
Hokusai's print of the mountain appears on the back of the new 1,000-yen note issued in 2024.

landmark-053.summary: A Kyoto temple, converted from a shogun's villa, whose gold-leaf pavilion is mirrored in a pond.
facts: The villa was acquired in 1397 by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu; the temple's official name is Rokuon-ji.
A young monk burned it down in 1950; it was rebuilt in 1955, and Yukio Mishima turned the story into a novel.

landmark-054.summary: Opened in 2012 and standing 634 meters, the tallest broadcasting tower in the world.
facts: The height of 634 is a pun on Musashi, the area's old province name.
It has observation decks at 350 and 450 meters and took over TV broadcasting from Tokyo Tower in 2013.

landmark-055.summary: The main royal palace and the first one Joseon built in its capital, Hanyang, in 1395.
facts: Visitors wearing hanbok get in free.
Burned during the Imjin War in 1592, it lay empty for more than 270 years until it was rebuilt under King Gojong.

landmark-056.summary: A temple at the foot of Mount Toham in Gyeongju, said to have been greatly expanded by Kim Dae-seong in 751.
facts: The pagoda on the front of South Korea's 10-won coin is this temple's Dabotap.
In 1995, it became a World Heritage Site together with Seokguram Grotto.

landmark-057.summary: An observation and broadcasting tower on a mountain in the middle of the city.
facts: It was completed as a transmission tower in 1975, but security concerns kept it closed to the public until 1980.
The love locks on the observation deck railings have become a famous sight.

landmark-058.summary: The world's tallest building at 828 meters, opened in Dubai in 2010.
facts: On opening day, it was renamed from Burj Dubai in honor of the President of the United Arab Emirates.
The 163-story tower is where Tom Cruise scaled the outside wall himself in “Mission: Impossible.”

landmark-059.summary: An ancient Nabataean city carved out of red sandstone cliffs.
facts: At the end of a narrow gorge, Al-Khazneh, featured in “Indiana Jones,” comes into view.
It grew rich by charging tolls on caravans carrying frankincense and spices.

landmark-060.summary: The remains of a Persian royal palace that Darius I began building around 518 BC.
facts: It was burned after Alexander the Great captured it in 330 BC.
Reliefs depicting processions of tribute bearers still survive.

landmark-061.summary: A 508-meter skyscraper modeled on the segments of a bamboo stalk, opened in 2004.
facts: Its elevators climb more than 1,000 meters per minute.
Visitors can see the 660-ton steel damper ball suspended between the 88th and 92nd floors.

landmark-062.summary: The world's highest peak, rising 8,848.86 meters above sea level on the border of Nepal and China.
facts: In 1977, Ko Sang-don became the first South Korean to stand on the summit.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first ascent in 1953.

landmark-063.summary: A group of colossal four-sided stone monuments built as tombs for three pharaohs: Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure.
facts: They are the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
Khufu's alone is thought to contain more than 2 million stone blocks.

landmark-064.summary: A stone statue with a lion's body and a human head, thought by some to bear the face of King Khafre.
facts: It sits beside the pyramids, gazing east.
Its nose had already fallen off centuries before Napoleon's army arrived.

landmark-065.summary: A temple carved into a rocky mountainside by the Nile by Ramesses II in the 13th century BC.
facts: Threatened with flooding by the construction of the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s, it was moved in its entirety and rebuilt.
Every year around February 22 and October 22, sunlight reaches the statues in its innermost sanctuary.

landmark-066.summary: A temple on the east bank of the Nile built by Amenhotep III and Ramesses II.
facts: One of its pair of obelisks now stands in Paris.
A 2.7-kilometer avenue of sphinxes once linked it to the Karnak Temple.

landmark-067.summary: Africa's highest peak, 5,895 meters tall and capped with snow despite lying near the equator.
facts: Trails lead to the top without technical climbing skills, so tens of thousands attempt it every year.
It is the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.

landmark-068.summary: A vast grassland where herds of wildebeest migrate every year in search of water and grass.
facts: Its name means “endless plains.”
It forms a single ecosystem with Kenya's Maasai Mara.

landmark-069.summary: A Kenyan national safari reserve bordering the Serengeti.
facts: “Mara” means “spotted” in the Maasai language.
From July to October, safari vehicles flock to watch herds of wildebeest cross the Mara River.

landmark-070.summary: The site of a seafaring city founded by the Phoenicians that fought three wars against Rome.
facts: It fell to Rome in 146 BC, at the end of the third of the Punic Wars.
Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, its name means “New City.”

landmark-071.summary: An old-town square that fills with food stalls and performers after sunset.
facts: It is the central square of the medina, the old quarter of Marrakesh.
In 2001, UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

landmark-072.summary: A rocky massif rising behind Cape Town, its long summit stretching out perfectly flat.
facts: The summit stands 1,085 meters high and can be reached by cable car.
The white cloud that spills over the top is called the “tablecloth.”

landmark-073.summary: A rocky headland on the southwestern coast of Africa that became a key waypoint on the sea route to India during the Age of Discovery.
facts: Bartolomeu Dias first reached it in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms.
Africa's southernmost point is actually Cape Agulhas.

landmark-074.summary: An ancient city in southern Africa built of stone by the ancestors of the Shona people between the 11th and 15th centuries.
facts: The country's name and the bird emblem on its flag both come from these ruins.
Its walls were built of fitted stones without any mortar.

landmark-075.summary: A statue in New York Harbor, a gift from France to mark the centennial of American independence.
facts: It was unveiled in 1886, and its internal iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
The tablet in its left hand is inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence.

landmark-076.summary: A vast red gorge carved by the Colorado River over countless ages.
facts: In places, it is more than 1,800 meters deep.
Its rock layers record nearly 2 billion years of Earth's history.

landmark-077.summary: A suspension bridge painted a reddish orange, spanning the entrance to San Francisco Bay.
facts: It opened in 1937, and its anti-rust primer, “International Orange,” was kept as its final color.
With a 1,280-meter main span, it was the world's longest suspension bridge until 1964.

landmark-078.summary: The residence in Washington, D.C., completed in 1800, where the President of the United States lives and works.
facts: In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt made “White House” its official name.
The president's office, the Oval Office, is in the West Wing.

landmark-079.summary: A sculpture of four presidents' faces carved into a granite cliff in the Black Hills between 1927 and 1941.
facts: It is the setting of the final chase scene in Hitchcock's “North by Northwest.”
About 400 people worked on it, and most of the rock was removed with dynamite.

landmark-080.summary: The world's first national park, where geysers and hot springs bubble up from the ground.
facts: It was designated a national park in 1872.
Old Faithful geyser shoots water more than 40 meters into the air roughly every 90 minutes.

landmark-081.summary: A 553-meter observation tower overlooking Lake Ontario.
facts: It has an observation level with a glass floor.
After opening in 1976, it was the world's tallest free-standing structure until 2007.

landmark-082.summary: Canada's first national park, in the Rocky Mountains, famous for its jade-colored lakes.
facts: Lake Louise gets its turquoise color from glacial rock flour.
Railway workers found hot springs here in 1883, and after disputes over who owned them, the area became a protected reserve in 1885.

landmark-083.summary: A Maya site dominated by the step pyramid known as El Castillo.
facts: At the spring and fall equinoxes, a serpent-shaped shadow appears on its stairway.
Its four stairways of 91 steps each, plus the top platform, add up to 365.

landmark-084.summary: An ancient city where the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon line a grand avenue.
facts: It had already been abandoned by the time the Aztecs discovered it.
Its central avenue is called the Avenue of the Dead.

landmark-085.summary: A man-made waterway with locks that links the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
facts: Opened in 1914, it spared ships the long voyage around Cape Horn at the tip of South America.
New locks opened in 2016 to let larger ships through.

landmark-086.summary: The remains of a stone city built by the Inca on a ridge in the Andes in the mid-15th century.
facts: It sits at about 2,430 meters above sea level, and the number of visitors allowed each day is capped.
It became widely known to the outside world in 1911 through Hiram Bingham.

landmark-087.summary: Giant drawings of animals and geometric shapes etched into the desert floor.
facts: Hard to make out from the ground, they became known to the world in the 1920s and '30s when planes flew over them.
They have survived so long because it almost never rains there.

landmark-088.summary: A giant statue of Jesus with outstretched arms, looking down over Rio de Janeiro.
facts: It stands on the summit of Corcovado mountain.
Completed in 1931, it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

landmark-089.summary: A white expanse of salt that mirrors the sky perfectly when covered by a thin layer of water.
facts: It is the largest salt flat in the world.
It holds the world's largest deposits of lithium, used in batteries for electric cars and smartphones.

landmark-090.summary: Giant stone statues with human faces, lined up with their backs to the sea on a remote island in the South Pacific.
facts: More than 900 statues have been found on the island so far.
Most were carved from volcanic tuff at Rano Raraku.

landmark-091.summary: A volcanic archipelago in the Pacific where Charles Darwin found clues that led to his theory of evolution.
facts: The finches on each island have differently shaped beaks.
Giant tortoises and marine iguanas live here.

landmark-092.summary: The world's highest waterfall, plunging from the top of a flat-topped mountain.
facts: It drops 979 meters and inspired Paradise Falls in the movie “Up.”
It is named after aviator Jimmie Angel, who first flew over it in 1933.

landmark-093.summary: A performing arts center opened in 1973 at the tip of a harbor point, with white roofs that look like billowing sails.
facts: It was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who resigned in 1966 and never saw it completed.
The more than 1.05 million tiles covering its white roofs were made by a Swedish company.

landmark-094.summary: A massive rock rising alone from the middle of the red desert.
facts: It is sacred to the Aboriginal Anangu people and is also known as Ayers Rock, a name given by an explorer in 1873.
Climbing it has been banned since October 2019.

landmark-095.summary: The world's largest coral system, visible even from space.
facts: It stretches for 2,300 kilometers.
When water temperatures rise, the corals turn white and die in a process called bleaching.

landmark-096.summary: A fjord on the South Island, enclosed by sheer cliffs and waterfalls.
facts: It rains so often that waterfalls form on every cliff face.
Rudyard Kipling called it the eighth wonder of the world.
